text: Hi, I'm
Ramona J. Smith, Toastmasters International  2018 World Champion of Public Speaking.
You may know the feeling of nervousness or even  anxiety that happens when you have to speak in
front of others without time to prepare.  Maybe for an unexpected question during a
job interview or maybe when a teacher called  on you in class when your hand wasn't raised.
In your professional life, you may have even  been asked to fill in for someone else during
a meeting. I know first-hand that being put on  the spot is an intimidating speaking challenge.
Yet I'm one of millions of people  who Toastmasters has helped gain the
confidence to communicate in all circumstances. Impromptu speaking is a skill that everyone
can benefit from. It can help you in social  situations, such as weddings and birthdays,
or even at work or school. We'll start  by looking at the times you might have
an opportunity to speak, then we'll move on  to techniques to manage last-minute speeches.
Practice impromptu speaking. Let's begin with the many opportunities
to practice speaking spontaneously.  Meetings at work or in the classroom,
whether they re virtual or in-person, can  help you test your impromptu speaking skills.
There are many other common everyday opportunities  to practice as well, such as speaking with a bank
teller, customer service representative, or even  someone in line with you at the grocery store.
You might be invited to attend a  wedding, retirement, or engagement party.
These events are perfect opportunities to  practice impromptu speaking from the heart.
Techniques
Now that we've pinpointed a few  potential places of practice,
let's take a closer look at the techniques  to help you manage your impromptu speaking.
The first approach is a simple formula  known as PREP, which stands for: Point,
Reason, Example, Point. Start your speech by
making a clear point about a subject. For  example, Internet outages are annoying.
Next, explain why you are speaking on the  topic, then give a few examples to bring
life to your story, and, finally, end with a  concluding point that wraps up your speech.
Those might include things like,  I m speaking on this topic because
it happened today and that is why I am at the  market, waiting in this long line. After that,
you might add another anecdote[A8] and finally,  a conclusion about internet unreliability.
By following this flow, you'll be able  to clearly state your main point and help
keep your ideas on course. PREP is an excellent fit
for more professional settings such as  business meetings and even interviews.
Another way to manage your speaking  time is by following the pros vs. cons,
or positive and negative method. Set up an issue by addressing the
pros first, the cons second, and then neatly  wrap up your point with your recommendation.
Pros vs. cons also works well in a professional  setting and in many every-day settings as well.
Filling in for a speaker If you find yourself filling in
for a speaker, quickly think about how you  would open and close your speech. You may
begin by sharing a few personal stories, and then  engaging the audience by acting as a moderator.
You can encourage questions and answers  to extend the speaking time if needed.
Now that you've considered how  to prepare for your speech,
it's time to concentrate on the final and most  important step: delivering your impromptu speech.
The only way to master impromptu speaking is  by jumping in and practicing in real-time.
If you struggle with being a perfectionist,  don't stress. Simply try to have fun. Most
people at the event will applaud your  courage and willingness to stand in.
